evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# dsh-ai-memory

**Memory bridge between DeepSeek Harness and ai-memory.**

[ai-memory](https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory) shares one memory across
20+ coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and more
all read and write the same wiki. DSH could only ever *read* it. This plugin
makes DSH a **full writer** too.

---

## What this is not

Read this first, because it decides whether this package is for you.

- **It is not ai-memory.** ai-memory is a separate project by a different
  author. This plugin does not contain it, does not bundle it, and does not
  replace it.
- **It is not a fork of ai-memory.** There is no shared code and no git
  relationship. ai-memory is written in Rust; this plugin is a single ~800-line
  JavaScript file that *calls* the `ai-memory` command-line program you install
  yourself. See [Credits](#credits).
- **It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or supported by ai-memory's
  author.** It is an independent third-party integration.
- **It does not capture anything.** It only *finalizes* sessions that ai-memory
  has **already** captured. Capture comes from DSH hook wiring that you install
  separately — see [Prerequisites](#prerequisites).

## Credits

The memory engine this plugin drives is entirely the work of others:

> **[akitaonrails/ai-memory](https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory)** — MIT
> licensed. One Rust binary that captures agent sessions through lifecycle
> hooks, consolidates them into a searchable Markdown wiki, and serves that
> memory to 20+ harnesses over MCP and HTTP.

**No ai-memory code is included here.** This repository contains zero lines
taken from that project. It is a DSH-side adapter that shells out to the
`ai-memory` binary, nothing more. If this plugin is useful to you, the credit
belongs upstream — please star their repository.

## Memory between harnesses

This is the point of the plugin, so it is worth stating precisely.

ai-memory is built on the idea that memory should follow *you*, not your editor.
Quit Claude Code mid-task, open Codex in the same directory, and the next agent
picks up a real handoff. That works because every harness writes into one shared
store, and session-end consolidation turns the raw record into readable wiki
pages the next agent can search.

DSH was the odd one out. ai-memory's consolidation is triggered by a **session
end** event, and DSH never fires one — its session-terminating path exits
through a signal that emits no disposal event at all. So DSH sessions landed in
ai-memory as raw observations and **stopped there**:

```
Claude Code session ends ──► consolidated ──► wiki page ──► readable by every harness
DSH session ends         ──► raw observations only ──► invisible to every harness
```

DSH could search the memory other agents wrote, but nothing DSH did ever became
memory the others could read. One-way, in the wrong direction.

This plugin closes that loop by firing the finalize step DSH never fires. With
it installed:

```
DSH session ends ──► this plugin ──► ai-memory finalize-session ──► wiki page
                                                                      │
              Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, … ◄────────────┘
```

A DSH session becomes a page that Claude Code can retrieve, that a teammate's
Codex can search, that shows up in the next agent's handoff brief. **DSH stops
being a read-only consumer of the shared memory and becomes a peer writer in
it.**

That is the whole value: not a new memory system, but one harness joining an
existing one properly.

## Prerequisites

Two things must already work. The plugin will not do either of them for you.

**1. A running ai-memory server with capture wired into DSH.**

Install ai-memory from [upstream](https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory),
then wire DSH's lifecycle hooks so events are captured. ai-memory >=3.2.0
supports DSH natively; earlier versions need the legacy Claude Code bridge
configuration. A manual, single-command-string example supporting older servers
is in [`docs/hooks-dsh.json`](docs/hooks-dsh.json); see its native migration notes.

Verify capture independently before blaming this plugin:

```sh
ai-memory status          # sessions and observations should be increasing
ai-memory doctor          # inside your project directory
```

**2. The `ai-memory` CLI on the same machine.**

That is all. It resolves its own data directory and server URL, so the default
configuration needs no settings at all.

If the server is not running, this plugin logs a clear warning at startup and
does nothing else. Capture failing is a separate problem with a separate cause.

## Install

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-ai-memory
```

From GitHub instead of npm:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add github:rasyidmmz/dsh-ai-memory
```

Restart DSH afterwards. The loader imports plugin code without a cache-buster,
so an edited or newly added plugin is not picked up until the process restarts.

Confirm it loaded by searching the harness log for `ai-memory`:

```
[dsh-ai-memory] active v1.2.0 -- fast path session/disposed (zero idle cost) + ...
[dsh-ai-memory] preflight: ai-memory v3.1.1 | data_dir=... | server=127.0.0.1:49374
```

The preflight line is the fastest way to confirm the plugin found the same
ai-memory your hooks are writing to.

### From the DSH marketplace — the half this plugin does not bring

Installing from a marketplace gives you the **finalize** half in one row. Two
things are still yours to provide, and the startup log now names whichever one
is missing instead of looking merely idle:

1. **ai-memory itself.** The plugin shells out to the `ai-memory` binary; it does
   not bundle or install it. When the binary is missing the log says so, with the
   install link and the `exePath` key that overrides the expected location, and
   nothing is finalized until it appears.
2. **Capture hooks.** ai-memory only knows about a DSH session if DSH forwards
   lifecycle events to it. That wiring is one `insert:` row in the profile's
   `cordis.patch.yml` pointing `@deepseek-ai/dsh-hooks-claude-code` at a hooks
   file; the reference file ships in this package as
   [`docs/hooks-dsh.json`](docs/hooks-dsh.json). Without it ai-memory records no
   DSH sessions at all — so there is nothing to finalize, and the log says
   exactly that, with the path to that template.

   The plugin deliberately does **not** write that row for you. The desktop
   profile reloads `cordis.patch.yml` live, so writing it from inside a running
   harness is how people hang their app; and a second hooks row sitting next to
   one you already have would capture every session twice.

When both are in place, the preflight is one line and the rest is silent.

## Configuration

Optional. The defaults are correct for a standard ai-memory install, and the
plugin behaves identically with no `config:` block at all.

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: ai-memory
      name: dsh-ai-memory
      config:
        exePath: /usr/local/bin/ai-memory   # default: platform standard location
        dataDir: /home/me/.local/share/ai-memory  # default: let the CLI decide
        # agentKind: dsh                     # optional pin; must match capture hooks
        sweep: true                         # default: true
        preflight: true                     # default: true
        timeoutMs: 120000                   # default: 120000
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `exePath` | Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ai-memory\ai-memory.exe`; elsewhere: `ai-memory` from `PATH` | Path to the ai-memory executable. |
| `dataDir` | unset | ai-memory data directory. **Leave unset** unless you use a non-standard location; the CLI then resolves its own, which is what the hooks use. |
| `agentKind` | stored session kind, falling back to `claude-code` | An explicit value pins finalization to that capture identity. Leave unset for mixed legacy/native stores. |
| `sweep` | `true` | The abandoned-session safety net. Set `false` to disable it entirely. |
| `preflight` | `true` | Log one line at startup naming the ai-memory version, data directory, and server it found. |
| `timeoutMs` | `120000` | Per-`finalize-session` timeout. |

### Legacy and native DSH capture

ai-memory **3.2.0** added `AgentKind::Dsh` and migration V85. Its DSH support is
now listed as **Hooks + MCP**. Earlier releases require `--agent claude-code`.
The UUID mapping is unchanged.

A server upgrade does **not** change the identity written by existing hooks.
This plugin therefore reads each session's `agent_kind` from the local store
(read-only), accepting only `dsh` and `claude-code`. That identity stays fixed
through all project fallbacks and `--reopen`. Preflight never changes it.
The sweeper also excludes unrelated harness kinds before applying its existing
live-session, idle-time and UUIDv5 guards.

If the row/store or `node:sqlite` is unavailable, finalization falls back to
`claude-code`, matching the shipped legacy hook template. For native capture on
a remote-only store, explicitly configure `agentKind: dsh`.

To opt into native capture, first upgrade ai-memory to **3.2.0 or later**, then
change every capture command in your hooks file from `--agent claude-code` to
`--agent dsh` and restart DSH (the bridge reads hooks once). Start a new session
and verify its stored identity. Leave plugin `agentKind` unset so old captured
sessions can still finalize as `claude-code`. The plugin does not rewrite hooks,
relabel database rows, or modify your profile patch.

## How it works

Two paths, deliberately asymmetric.

### Fast path — an event, costing nothing while idle

When a session closes cleanly, DSH fires `session/disposed`. The plugin listens,
derives the session's stored UUID, and calls `ai-memory finalize-session`.

- **Idle cost: zero.** No timer, no query, no process started.
- **Reaction: immediate**, not waiting for a scheduled sweep.

It uses `session/disposed` rather than the two events that fire alongside it
because it is the only one carrying the full session object, so the working
directory is read directly instead of being cached or guessed.

### Safety net — the tiered sweeper

DSH terminates through `SIGTERM`, and `SIGTERM` fires **no** disposal event at
all. A session open at that moment is never finalized: it stays open forever
with no page. This is not hypothetical — one session with 459 observations was
left behind that way.

So a sweeper exists that depends on no event: it reads ai-memory's store
directly and finalizes sessions that are provably dead. Its schedule is dense at
first and then eases off — 25s, 1 min, 3 min, 10 min, then every 30 min —
because the only case an event misses is a session abandoned by a restart, which
happens right when DSH starts.

Getting this wrong is worse than not doing it: finalizing a **live** session
produces a page from half its content, and that page is never updated again. So
four guards must all pass:

1. the session is not in this process's live-session list;
2. its last observation is more than 2 minutes old;
3. its UUID is version 5 — main sessions only, never subagents;
4. at most 10 sessions per sweep.

Guard 2 covers a second DSH window: that is a separate process, so its session
is invisible here, and without the delay it would be closed mid-write.

Guard 3 has a useful side effect worth knowing if you run DSH alongside real
Claude Code sessions in one repository: ai-memory stores those as version-4
UUIDs, so they can never be selected by this sweeper.

Set `sweep: false` to turn the whole net off; the fast path is unaffected.

### The seven traps this solves

Each of these broke an earlier version, and each fix is load-bearing. They are
worth listing because they are the reason a naive "just call finalize-session"
plugin does not work.

1. **The session id is not a raw UUID.** DSH ids look like `session-<uuid>` and
   ai-memory stores them as a derived UUID v5. Passing the raw string is
   rejected: `invalid uuid: invalid character: found 's' at 1`. Child agents use
   a bare UUID and must be passed *as is* — two id shapes, two treatments.
2. **The working directory must be explicit.** The shell service defaults to the
   DSH process's own directory, not the session's repository, so scope resolves
   to the wrong project.
3. **The project name is not always the folder's basename.** Hooks write it
   lowercased; the CLI derives it with original casing. Repositories without an
   `.ai-memory.toml` marker only match after a lowercase retry.
4. **No `2>&1`.** DSH runs commands with stderr unredirected, and collapsing it
   inside the command fails there, exiting non-zero having done nothing.
5. **Subagent detection must read the session header, not the registry.** The
   agent registry deletes an entry *before* announcing its disposal, so a
   registry lookup is always empty — including for the main session. An earlier
   version used it as a filter and therefore skipped every agent, doing nothing
   at all while logging no error.
6. **Concurrent session ends must queue, not drop.** Closing DSH with two
   sessions open fires two disposal events back to back; a naive `running` guard
   silently discards the second.
7. **`SIGTERM` fires nothing** — hence the sweeper above.

## Troubleshooting

All output is prefixed `[dsh-ai-memory]`. Search the harness log for it.

The prefix deliberately is not `[ai-memory]`: ai-memory has its own logs, and an
identical prefix makes it impossible to tell whose line you are reading.

| Log line | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `active v1.1.0 ...` | Plugin loaded | — |
| `preflight: ai-memory vX \| data_dir=...` | Found the server | Confirm the data directory matches your hooks |
| `WARNING: ai-memory executable not found` | Wrong `exePath` | Set `exePath` in config |
| `preflight: the ai-memory server did not answer` | Server not running | Start ai-memory |
| `sandbox runner is broken (0xC0000142)` | DSH's sandbox runner is failing under Electron; the plugin switched to the unconfined path | See "Sandbox runner" below. Sessions still finalize |
| `session ... -> page created` | Working | — |
| `session ... -> no open session matched` | Already finalized, or never captured | Check `ai-memory status`; if observations are not rising, the **hooks** are the problem, not this plugin |
| `session ... FAILED` | The CLI returned an error | The message tail is included |
| `sweeper could not read the store` | ai-memory's schema changed | The fast path keeps working; only the safety net is down |
| `sweeper: no abandoned sessions` | Normal, most sweeps | — |

If nothing appears at all, the plugin is not loaded — check the profile's
`cordis.patch.yml` and restart DSH.

> **Note on `finalize-session` and consolidation.** This plugin calls
> `finalize-session`, which is a client of the running server. It does not
> invoke an LLM and does not write wiki pages itself; the server does that. If
> pages are not appearing, check the server's own logs.

## Compatibility

- **DSH**: developed and tested against DSH Desktop **`0.2.1-rc.2`**
  (the `@deepseek-ai/dsh-desktop` package), Node 24. Re-verified on 0.2.1-rc.2
  on 2026-10-18 from the installed `app.asar`: `agent/created`,
  `agent/disposed` and `session/disposed` are still emitted, `ctx.sessions.get()`
  still returns a session whose `header` carries `cwd`, `origin` and
  `delegationDepth`, and `ctx.shell` still exposes `execute()` only (the
  `run()`-then-`execute()` capability branch below covers both). 1.0.4 and
  1.1.1 were verified on `0.2.0-rc.2`.

  > Earlier revisions of this README said "DSH Desktop 0.9.1". That was wrong —
  > no such DSH version exists. `0.9.1` had been read off an unrelated
  > changelog; the package version at the time was `0.1.7-rc.2`. Revisions
  > 1.0.0-1.0.3 were tested on `0.1.7-rc.2`.

- **ai-memory**: developed against **2.5.2** (upgraded from 2.4.0 through
  2.5.2, each verified working end-to-end), re-verified on **3.1.1** on
  2026-10-18. What was actually checked, not assumed:
  - `finalize-session` still accepts `--agent`, `--workspace`, `--project`,
    `--session-id`, `--reopen` and `--json`;
  - its output lines are unchanged — `Finalized …` on success and
    `No open … sessions matched …` when there is nothing to close, which is
    what this plugin's classification reads;
  - session ids are still `uuid5(NAMESPACE_OID, native id)`
    (`crates/ai-memory-core/src/ids.rs:94`), the exact mapping
    `sessionIdToUuid` reproduces;
  - a 2.6-era store opens under 3.1.1: it migrated to schema **V83** without
    error, and the sweeper's query returns the same rows afterwards;
  - `status --json` still exists and still reports `version`, `data_dir` and
    `bind`, which the startup preflight prints.
  `--reopen` and the marker's `identity` key arrived in 2.5.0 and are used by
  1.1.0+. See the compatibility notes below for what the upgrades changed.
- **Platforms**: Windows is the tested platform. Linux and macOS command
  construction is implemented and exercised, but not run end-to-end by the
  author — treat those as untested.
- **No dependencies.** No `dependencies`, no `peerDependencies`, so there is no
  build step and no `allowBuilds` approval on install.
- **No tools, no UI.** The plugin registers no model tools and draws no
  interface. It only listens and shells out.

### Upgrading the ai-memory *server* from 2.x to 3.x

The CLI contract this plugin uses did not change, but the **server** may refuse
to start after the jump, and that failure looks like the plugin's fault because
finalize calls then fail with a connection error. Observed on the author's
machine going 2.6.0 → 3.1.1 against a copy of the store:

```
provider not configured: no openai-oauth token found at <data-dir>\auth.json;
run `ai-memory auth login openai-oauth`
```

2.6.0 was serving with an `openai-compat` provider configured through
`llm_base_url` plus environment keys; 3.1.1 wants a credential file for that
provider route. The **store migrated cleanly** (schema V83, same pages,
sessions and observations) — so this is a provider/auth step, not data loss.
Run the `ai-memory auth login …` command the message names (or point the config
at a still-valid `api_key_env`) before restarting the service, then check
`ai-memory status` again.

### ai-memory 2.4.0 → 2.4.1

The upgrade was run and verified on the author's machine; nothing broke. The
store kept every page, session and observation, and embeddings improved
(6 pages missing → 0). Two entries in that release are worth knowing here:

- **CRLF pages are read correctly again** — a page saved by a Windows editor
  used to load without its frontmatter (`pinned` / `expires_at` silently lost).
  Relevant on Windows, which is the tested platform.
- **Session ids no longer split on letter case** — `D:\…\Default Project` could
  become two separate projects. On an affected store, this release merges them.

### Two shell API shapes

The plugin calls `ctx.shell` through one helper that accepts **both** shapes:

| Harness | Call | Result |
|---|---|---|
| older | `shell.run(spec)` | `{ exitCode, stdout, stderr }` |
| DSH 0.1.7-rc.2 | `shell.execute(spec)` | handle, then `handle.result()` |

This is detected by capability (`typeof ctx.shell.execute`), never by version
number, so a future rename cannot silently break it again. It matters because
`PwshLocalExecutor` in 0.1.7-rc.2 exposes **only** `execute()`: without the
branch, every finalize dies with `shell.run is not a function` — and because the
failure only reaches the log, it looks like "the plugin is loaded but nothing
happens" rather than an error.

### Sandbox runner

DSH 0.1.7-rc.2 launches its sandbox runner through Electron, and the confined
child process dies with `STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED` (`0xC0000142`). Measured
directly, same command, correct SID:

| Launcher | Result |
|---|---|
| `node.exe` + runner | `exit=0` (works) |
| `DeepSeek Harness.exe` + runner | `exit=3221225794` (`0xC0000142`) |

A plugin's `ctx.shell` calls carry no session, so they fall back to the default
`workspace-write` policy and always take the broken path.

The plugin therefore tries the **normal, confined** path first and falls back
only when it sees `0xC0000142`, remembering the switch. The moment DSH fixes its
runner, finalize returns to being sandboxed with no change needed here.

**Be aware of the trade-off:** the fallback widens the CLI call's permissions
beyond the workspace (`danger-full-access`). It is contained to the
`ai-memory finalize-session` invocation — not the agent's own tools — and the
plugin never writes files itself. If that is not acceptable in your setup, do not
run it on a harness with a broken runner; there is no config switch to disable
the fallback in 1.0.2.


### If ai-memory changes

The plugin reads ai-memory's SQLite store directly in **one** place, the
sweeper, and only to *find* abandoned sessions. If a future ai-memory release
changes that schema, the sweeper logs an error and stops; the fast path is
untouched because it uses no SQL at all. Set `sweep: false` to silence it
entirely in that case.

## License

MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). This license covers **this plugin only**.
ai-memory is separately licensed (also MIT) by its own author.

# dsh-plugin-reactive-resume Connect [Reactive Resume](https://rxresu.me) to [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). Read, create, and edit your resumes and job applications from a Harness session. ## Install ```bash dsh plugin --profile add dsh-plugin-reactive-resume ``` This package declares `dsh.bundle`, so the profile picks it up as a layer and mounts it automatically. Until you configure a key it mounts nothing and logs a warning, so installing it never leaves a profile unbootable. ## Configure Mint an API key at `https://rxresu.me/dashboard/settings/api-keys` and export it as `RXRESUME_API_KEY` — the bundle patch reads that variable. To set it explicitly, or to change any other option, patch the row by id from your profile's `cordis.patch.yml`: ```yaml - id: reactive-resume config: apiKey: !!js process.env.RXRESUME_API_KEY ``` ### Options | Key | Default | Description | | ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `apiKey` | `''` | API key from `/dashboard/settings/api-keys`. Empty mounts nothing. | | `url` | `https://rxresu.me` | Origin of your instance. Set this if you self-host. | | `serverName` | `resume` | Tool namespace. Tools reach the model as `mcp____`. | | `toolCallTimeoutMs` | `60000` | Per-tool-call timeout. | Every tool Reactive Resume publishes is exposed. Narrowing that set is not currently possible from a plugin: Harness's `ctx.tools.restrict()` requires an agent-scoped context, which a plugin context is not. ### Self-hosted ```yaml - id: reactive-resume config: apiKey: !!js process.env.RXRESUME_API_KEY url: http://localhost:3000 ``` ## What it does Bridges Reactive Resume's MCP server into `ctx.tools`, and contributes a system-prompt section covering the things models get wrong about resume editing: reading before patching, RFC 6902 path construction against the published schema, UUID-keyed section entries, and locked resumes. You could wire the bridge yourself with a raw `@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client` row. What you cannot do that way is contribute the prompt section — that is what this package adds. ## Harness compatibility The peer ranges list each supported DSH host line as an explicit `||` union: `^0.1.0-rc.6` (what this package already shipped against) plus `^0.2.0-rc.1` (which admits `0.2.0-rc.1` and `0.2.0-rc.2`). The union is purely additive — every version the old range admitted is still admitted. Every published DSH release is a prerelease, which makes the comparison mode matter: - The Harness host decides whether to mount a plugin with `semver.satisfies(runtime, range, { includePrerelease: true })`. The upper bound is what rejected the old range there: `^0.1.0-rc.6` expands to `>=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0`, and `0.2.0-rc.2` sorts above `0.2.0-0` because the numeric identifier `0` precedes `rc`. - npm's default mode — the one the plugin market's checker uses — additionally requires a comparator set to pin the same `major.minor.patch` tuple with a prerelease of its own. Under that mode the bare `^0.1.0-rc.6` admits only `0.1.0-rc.6` through `0.1.0-rc.8`. Measured against all 29 published host releases, that gap is wide: `^0.1.0-rc.6` admits 22 of them under the host's mode (every `0.1.x` line, including `0.1.5-rc.2` and `0.1.7-rc.2`) but only 3 under npm's default mode. Widening the upper bound does not close it, because the default mode ignores the widened comparator: `>=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.3.0-0` still admits only those same 3, and `*` admits none at all. `^0.1.0-rc.6 || ^0.2.0-rc.1` admits 24 releases under the host's mode and 5 under the default one, so an explicit union member per host line is the only form both checkers agree on. Against `0.2.0-rc.2` this package needed no source change: `dsh-mcp-client@0.2.0-rc.2` keeps its `Config` union, its `apply(ctx, config)` signature, and the `mcp____` public tool name, while `dsh-system-prompt@0.2.0-rc.2` keeps `section({ name, order, text })`. What 0.2.0 adds to the bridge — MCP resource publishing and a server-instructions prompt section — is additive and scoped to `ctx.inject(["mcpResources"])` / `ctx.inject(["systemPrompt"])`, neither of which this package depends on. ## Development This package lives in the [Reactive Resume monorepo](https://github.com/reactive-resume/reactive-resume) at `packages/dsh-plugin`, next to `packages/mcp` — the server it bridges. `src/tool-names.test.ts` checks every tool the prompt guide names against `@reactive-resume/mcp/tool-names`, so renaming a tool breaks this package in the same pull request. ```bash pnpm --filter dsh-plugin-reactive-resume test pnpm --filter dsh-plugin-reactive-resume build ``` ## License MIT > [!IMPORTANT] > Reactive Resume now lives at **[`reactive-resume/reactive-resume`](https://github.com/reactive-resume/reactive-resume)** on GitHub. > GHCR images publish to `ghcr.io/reactive-resume/reactive-resume`. > Docker Hub stays at `amruthpillai/reactive-resume`.

Reactive Resume

Reactive Resume is a free and open-source resume builder for writing resumes and cover letters, checking your work, and tracking job applications.

Get Started · Learn More

Sponsored by

--- Create a free account, import an existing resume or start fresh, and see the finished page as you write. Download a PDF, Word, Markdown, or JSON file, or share your resume with a public link. You can also run the whole application on your own infrastructure. You own your data. The codebase is open source under the MIT license, with no tracking, no ads, and no paid tier. Optional AI features use a provider you connect; hosting and provider usage may have their own costs. ![Reactive Resume v6 editor with Write, Design, and Check modes and a live PDF preview](docs/images/getting-started/editor-overview.webp) ## Build a better resume, together [Join the Reactive Resume community on Discord](https://discord.gg/u9pAd3za9t) to exchange resume feedback, get help using or self-hosting the app, and share ideas with other users and contributors. - **Resume feedback:** post a redacted resume and one specific question, or help someone improve theirs. - **Help:** find troubleshooting discussions and ask questions in dedicated forum threads. - **Contribute:** discuss ideas, translations, and code with the people building Reactive Resume. Feedback comes from fellow community members. Remove contact details and other private information before posting. ## Features **Write, Design, and Check** - Redesigned editor with inline content editing and click-to-select on the page - Live PDF preview and browser downloads powered by Forme, rendered in a background worker - Rich text, custom sections, drag-and-drop ordering, and structured dates with consistent formatting - Autosave, local recovery of unsaved resume drafts, and up to 200 undo steps - Phone and tablet layouts, keyboard shortcuts, and a searchable command bar **Templates and Customization** - 18 templates, including the new Porygon and Smeargle, previewed with your own content - One-column, two-column, and ATS-safe template filters - Font presets, custom fonts, colors, spacing, A4 and Letter paper, and left or right sidebars - Fit overflowing content by adjusting density, margins, and text size - Custom Styles written as Semantic CSS, with an element picker on the page **Resume Checks** - Readability checks with findings pinned to the relevant lines - Job-posting keyword matching and a view of the text hiring software reads - Checks on the exported PDF, plus an optional AI writing review - A public [ATS checker](https://rxresu.me/ats-checker) that reads PDFs in your browser without an account **Documents and Cover Letters** - One searchable library for resumes and letters, with tags, sorting, and grid or list views - Standalone cover letters with their own editor, exports, and version history - Link a letter to a resume to keep its sender details and design in sync, or customize it independently - Automatic and named versions you can preview and restore - Trash with Undo and a 30-day recovery window **Job Applications** - List, Board, Insights, and Calendar views for tracking applications from Saved to Offer - Save jobs from a URL or pasted posting; optional keyword search through Firecrawl, Tavily, or Exa - Tailor a resume and draft a cover letter for a saved job - Track contacts, notes, follow-ups, application outcomes, and the documents you sent - Schedule interviews, export calendar events, and import or export applications as CSV **AI Assistant** - Assistant beside your resume or letter, with conversations tied to that document - Proposed edits show what changes and why; accept or reject each suggestion - Improve selected text, review writing, and draft letters from a resume and job posting - Connect OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama, or other supported providers and compatible endpoints - Optional web search and page reading; self-hosters can configure shared AI and web-access providers **Import, Export, and Sharing** - Import Reactive Resume JSON, JSON Resume, LinkedIn data exports, PDF, and Word files - JSON, LinkedIn, and readable PDF imports work without AI; Word imports require a connected provider - Export resumes and letters as PDF, Word (DOCX), Markdown, or JSON - Share resumes through public links with optional password protection and view/download statistics - REST API and MCP server for document management, imports, exports, checks, and application workflows **Privacy and Control** - Self-host with Docker, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, or a 1-click deploy on Hostinger - No tracking or ads; export your account data or delete your account - Passkeys, two-factor authentication, and linked sign-in providers - Multiple interface languages, light/dark/system themes, and reduced-motion support ## Templates

## Quick Start Use the [hosted app](https://rxresu.me) to start writing, or build this checkout locally with Docker and Docker Compose: ```bash # Clone the repository git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/reactive-resume/reactive-resume.git reactive-resume cd reactive-resume # Create your local configuration cp .env.example .env # Edit .env: set AUTH_SECRET and a separate ENCRYPTION_SECRET. # Generate each secret with: openssl rand -hex 32 # Build the app and start PostgreSQL, Redis, and SeaweedFS docker compose up -d --build # Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser ``` This builds the checked-out source. For a deployment using published images, follow the [Docker guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/docker). For source development, see the [development setup guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/contributing/development). ## Tech Stack | Category | Technology | | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | Web app | React 19 SPA, TanStack Router, and Vite | | Server | Hono on Node.js 24 or Cloudflare Workers | | Language | TypeScript | | Monorepo | pnpm and Turborepo | | Database | PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM | | API | oRPC, OpenAPI REST, and MCP | | Auth | Better Auth | | Styling | Tailwind CSS | | UI Components | Base UI + shared UI package | | State Management | Zustand + TanStack Query | | PDF rendering | Forme, with PDF.js for the viewer | | Rich text | TipTap | | Localization | Lingui | ## Documentation The full documentation lives at [docs.rxresu.me](https://docs.rxresu.me): | Guide | Description | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | | [Getting started](https://docs.rxresu.me/getting-started) | First-time setup and basic usage | | [What's new in v6](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/whats-new-in-v6) | Changes and where familiar features moved | | [Checking your resume](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/checking-your-resume) | Readability, job match, and writing reviews | | [Using the assistant](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/using-the-assistant) | Ask for changes and review proposed edits | | [Writing a cover letter](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/writing-a-cover-letter) | Create a letter and link it to a resume | | [Tracking job applications](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/tracking-job-applications) | Saved jobs, stages, interviews, and insights | | [Exporting your resume](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/exporting-your-resume) | PDF, Word, Markdown, and JSON downloads | | [API](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/using-the-api) and [MCP](https://docs.rxresu.me/guides/using-the-mcp-server) | Connect scripts and external assistants | | [Self-hosting](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/docker) | Deploy on your own infrastructure | | [Migrating from v5](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/upgrading-to-v6) | Migrations and integration changes | | [Development setup](https://docs.rxresu.me/contributing/development) | Local development environment | | [Project architecture](https://docs.rxresu.me/contributing/architecture) | Codebase structure and package boundaries | ## Self-Hosting Reactive Resume runs the same application everywhere: PostgreSQL for data, plus storage for uploads. Pick the option that fits how much you want to manage. | Option | Best for | Guide | | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [Hostinger](#hostinger) | A ready-made VPS with no setup | [Hostinger guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/hostinger) | | [Vercel](#vercel) | Serverless, with managed database and storage | [Vercel guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/vercel) | | [Cloudflare Workers](#cloudflare-workers) | Workers, R2 and your own PostgreSQL | [Cloudflare guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/cloudflare) | | [Docker and Kubernetes](#docker-and-kubernetes) | Your own server, homelab or cluster | [Docker](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/docker) · [Kubernetes](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/kubernetes) | > **PDF generation in v6** uses Forme in the browser and on the server. No Browserless, Chromium, or external print service is needed. Legacy `PRINTER_*` and `BROWSERLESS_*` environment variables can be removed. ### Hostinger The quickest way to get going is a 1-click deploy on Hostinger, starting at $6.49/month. Their VPS plans include a ready-made Reactive Resume template that provisions the Docker environment and brings the app up for you, with weekly backups and a Docker manager UI included — so you can skip the setup entirely. See the [Hostinger guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/hostinger) for what the template sets up and what to configure afterwards, such as email, your own domain, and turning off sign-ups. ### Vercel [![Deploy with Vercel](https://vercel.com/button)](https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Freactive-resume%2Freactive-resume&project-name=reactive-resume&repository-name=reactive-resume&env=AUTH_SECRET%2CENCRYPTION_SECRET&envDescription=Generate+two+independent+secrets+with+openssl+rand+-hex+32.+Keep+these+values+across+deployments.&envLink=https%3A%2F%2Fdocs.rxresu.me%2Fself-hosting%2Fvercel&stores=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22integration%22%2C%22protocol%22%3A%22storage%22%2C%22integrationSlug%22%3A%22neon%22%2C%22productSlug%22%3A%22neon%22%7D%2C%7B%22type%22%3A%22integration%22%2C%22protocol%22%3A%22storage%22%2C%22integrationSlug%22%3A%22upstash%22%2C%22productSlug%22%3A%22upstash-kv%22%7D%2C%7B%22type%22%3A%22blob%22%2C%22access%22%3A%22private%22%7D%5D) Vercel provisions Neon PostgreSQL, private Blob storage, and Upstash Redis through its deployment wizard. Supply two persistent secrets and use the **Services** framework preset. Static assets run in the frontend service, and Hono serves the application routes and APIs from the backend service. See the [Vercel guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/vercel) for setup, limits, and optional SMTP/OAuth configuration. ### Cloudflare Workers Cloudflare deployment requires **Workers Paid** and uses Static Assets, private R2 storage, SQLite Durable Objects, and PostgreSQL through Hyperdrive. Supply an existing PostgreSQL database and apply migrations before deployment. See the [Cloudflare guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/cloudflare) for setup and runtime limits. ### Docker and Kubernetes The application needs: - **PostgreSQL** — Accounts, documents, applications, and assistant conversations - **Upload storage** — A persistent local directory or an S3-compatible bucket, such as SeaweedFS - **Redis** (optional) — Shared coordination across instances and resumable assistant replies - **SMTP** (optional) — Verification and password-reset emails Published releases are available from Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry (`latest` tracks the latest stable release): ```bash # Docker Hub docker pull amruthpillai/reactive-resume:latest # GitHub Container Registry docker pull ghcr.io/reactive-resume/reactive-resume:latest ``` See the [Docker guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/docker) or [Kubernetes guide](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/kubernetes) for complete instructions. Running on a NAS? See the [Synology and UGREEN guides](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/nas). ### Configuration Every setting is listed in the [environment variables reference](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/environment-variables). Self-hosters can also configure [shared AI and job-search services](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/job-search-and-ai) and [single sign-on](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/sso). ### Upgrading from v5 Back up your database and uploads and stop all v5 instances before applying v6 migrations. Old visual style rules require a manual conversion; API and MCP integrations also have changes. Follow [Migrating from v5](https://docs.rxresu.me/self-hosting/upgrading-to-v6). ## Support Reactive Resume is and always will be free and open source. If it has helped you land a job or saved you time, please consider supporting continued development:

Other ways to support: - Star this repository - Report reproducible bugs and suggest actionable features - Help other users in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/reactive-resume/reactive-resume/discussions/categories/q-a) - Improve documentation - Help with translations ## Star History ## Contributing Every contribution helps, whether it is a typo fix or a new feature. 1. Fork the repository 2. Create a feature branch (`git checkout -b feature/amazing-feature`) 3. Commit your changes using Conventional Commits (`git commit -m 'feat: add amazing feature'`) 4. Push to the branch (`git push origin feature/amazing-feature`) 5. evidence.readmeExcerpt:
贴吧阅读器

把百度贴吧的一整栋楼，读成一份带图的结构化材料。
DeepSeek Harness 插件 · 只读 · 不发言、不点赞、不签到、不关注

非官方项目，由社区成员独立开发维护，与 DeepSeek 官方无关。

登录状态、抽样方式、是否截断、图片压多大、请求多慢——设置页里改完即时生效。

目录 - [它能产出什么](#它能产出什么) - [安装](#安装) - [登录](#登录) - [工具](#工具) - [抽样策略](#抽样策略) - [配置](#配置) - [命令行](#命令行) - [为什么必须用浏览器](#为什么必须用浏览器) - [与 DSH 的集成方式](#与-dsh-的集成方式) - [安全](#安全) - [已知限制](#已知限制) - [项目结构](#项目结构) - [开发](#开发) - [彩蛋](#彩蛋) - [许可](#许可)
## 它能产出什么 给一个 `tid`，回一份按楼层顺序排好的材料： ```text 《示例帖子：一个关于融资的讨论》 楼主 用户甲 ｜ 全文 39 层 ｜ 抽取 39 层 【第 1 层 0% 用户甲 楼主】 示例帖子的主楼内容 [图1] [图 …/.dsh-tieba/images/1234567890/f1_1.jpg] 【第 3 层 5% 用户乙】 这是某一层楼的回复内容[表情:咧嘴笑] └ 楼中楼 2 条: · 用户丙: 这是楼中楼里的一条回复 ``` | 特性 | 说明 | |---|---| | 按楼层 | 图片紧跟所属楼层，楼中楼挂在楼层下面 | | 表情转中文 | `image_emoticon22` → `[表情:咧嘴笑]`，**不读图** | | 省上下文 | 头像、昵称挂件永久跳过 | | 图片 | 按像素面积等比压缩，默认返回绝对路径，可直接交给读图工具 | | 路径样式 | `DSH_TIEBA_PATH_STYLE`：默认绝对路径；`rel` 相对当前工作目录；`home` 输出 `~/...`（需调用方自行展开） | ## 安装 要求 **DSH ≥ 0.2.0**（已声明 `engines.dsh`，版本不匹配时整包被跳过而不是半加载）。 ```bash dsh plugin --profile add dsh-plugin-tieba ``` `` 换成你在用的那个：跑 `dsh web` 就是 `web`，桌面版是 `desktop`，`ls ~/.dsh/profiles` 能看到全部。 这条命令会同时写 `dependencies` 和 `dsh.profile.bundles`，**不用手工编辑**。装完重启 DSH，浏览器硬刷新一次。 > **升级插件后也要重启**（不只是第一次装）：工具 schema 是在启动时注册的，不重启会继续用旧的那份。旧版本有问题时，症状就是对话被 API 直接拒绝。 **浏览器**：插件要用真实浏览器渲染贴吧页面，但通常不用额外装——Windows / macOS 自带 Edge 或装了 Chrome 就够了。只有系统里找不到任何 chromium 系浏览器时（多见于干净的 Linux 服务器）： ```bash npx playwright-core install chromium --only-shell # 约 118 MB # 或者：sudo apt install chromium ``` `npm run check-browser` 可以看实际会选中哪个浏览器。
从源码安装（改代码时用） ```bash git clone https://github.com/referiw/dsh-plugin-tieba ~/dsh-plugin-tieba cd ~/.dsh/profiles/ && pnpm add link:~/dsh-plugin-tieba ``` 这条路直接调 pnpm，**不会**改 bundles，需要手工把 `"dsh-plugin-tieba"` 追加到该 profile `package.json` 的 `dsh.profile.bundles` 数组末尾。 Windows 上保存成 **UTF-8 无 BOM**——带 BOM 时 DSH 读配置会抛 `Unexpected token '\uFEFF'`。
## 登录 贴吧的登录态只能靠真实浏览器拿到。 **设置页（推荐）**：DSH → 设置 → 贴吧 → 重新扫码登录。二维码直接显示在页面里，扫完自动变「已登录」。 **命令行**：`node src/login.mjs` cookie 落在 `~/.dsh-tieba/cookies.json`（`0600`），可用 `DSH_TIEBA_HOME` 改目录。 ## 工具 | 工具 | 作用 | |---|---| | `tieba_thread` | 读一个帖子：拉全文 → 抽样 → 按楼层顺序返回 | | `tieba_status` | 登录态（贴吧 ID、昵称、头像） | | `tieba_bars` | 当前账号关注的吧 | ```jsonc // tieba_thread 的常用参数 { "tid": "1234567890", // 必填，来自 URL /p/ "refresh": false, // 忽略缓存重拉 "sampleMode": "dynamic", // dynamic | fixed | ratio | all "floors": 100, // sampleMode=fixed 时的层数 "ratio": 0.1, // sampleMode=ratio 时的比例 "truncateText": false, // 是否截断过长楼层 "maxTextChars": 2000, // 截断时每层保留字数 "imageMaxArea": 1200000 // 图片像素面积上限 } ``` ## 抽样策略 默认**动态抽样**：楼层越多比例越低，结果夹在 `[min, max]` 之间。 | 总楼层 | 抽多少 | 比例 | | ---: | ---: | ---: | | ≤ 50 | 全读 | 100% | | 100 | 65 | 65% | | 300 | 125 | 42% | | 1000 | 230 | 23% | | > 1000 | 300（封顶） | < 30% | **楼主楼层始终补齐**，不占抽样名额。匿名帖没有用户名可匹配，第 1 层恒判为楼主。 ## 配置 设置页可改，也可直接编辑 `~/.dsh-tieba/config.json`（即时生效，无需重启）。 | 键 | 默认 | 说明 | |---|---|---| | `sampleMode` | `dynamic` | 抽样方式 | | `sampleMin` / `sampleMax` | `50` / `300` | 动态抽样的上下界 | | `sampleFixed` / `sampleRatio` | `50` / `0.2` | fixed / ratio 模式的取值 | | `truncateText` | `false` | 是否截断过长楼层 | | `maxTextChars` | `2000` | 截断时保留的字数 | | `imageMaxArea` | `1200000` | 图片像素面积上限，超出等比缩小 | | `imageMaxWidth` / `imageMaxHeight` | `1280` / `2000` | 图片尺寸上限 | | `gapMs` | `4000` | 请求间隔（毫秒） | | `cacheTtlMs` | `600000` | 全文缓存有效期 | | `maxPages` | `30` | 单帖最多抓多少页 | ## 命令行 不想装插件也能直接用： ```bash tieba status # 登录态 tieba thread 1234567890 # 读帖 tieba thread 1234567890 --json # 结构化输出 ``` `tieba` 是包的 `bin`；没全局安装时用 `node src/cli.mjs status` 等效。 ## 为什么必须用浏览器 贴吧对**未登录**的请求一律回「百度安全验证」页，`fetch` / `curl` 连正文都拿不到——我试过模拟 Chrome / Safari / Edge 的 TLS 指纹（`curl_cffi`），全是 403。能拿到楼层内容的只有真实浏览器引擎。 另外三个坑是插件替你填掉的： - **桌面版是前端二次渲染**，经典选择器抓不到，必须走移动版 `/mo/q/m`； - **翻页不能复用会话**，同一上下文里连翻 `pn=0 → 30 → 60` 会被判成机器人弹验证码，必须一页一个上下文； - **`pn` 是楼层偏移不是页码**，写 `pn=2` 返回空页。 ## 与 DSH 的集成方式 | 面 | 用什么 | |---|---| | 工具 | `ctx.tools.register`：`tieba_thread` / `tieba_status` / `tieba_bars` | | 设置页 | 客户端插件 `ctx.slots.inject('settings.section', …)` | | HTTP | `ctx.webServer` 挂 `/tieba/api/*`（只服务设置页） | | 装配 | `dsh.bundle.patch` 插入 `id: tieba` 一行 | | 展示 | `locale/*.json` 的 `meta.title` / `meta.description` | ## 安全 `/tieba/api/*` 沿用 DSH 自己 `/api` 的信任模型：**认 Host，不认连接地址**。 - 默认只接受回环地址（`127.0.0.1` / `::1` / `localhost`）； - `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` 一律拒绝；带 `Origin` 时必须与 `Host` 同源（挡 CSRF）； - **公网 / 反向代理 / 网关插件部署**：请求的 Host 是你的域名。**如果 DSH 本身已经用 `--trusted-host <域名>` 启动（网关/反代部署必然配过），插件会自动沿用那份白名单**，不用额外配置；否则显式放行： ```bash export DSH_TIEBA_TRUSTED_HOST=tieba.example.com # 多个用逗号分隔 ``` 403 的响应体里会带上你的 Host 和这句提示，照着设置就行。为什么不看 `X-Forwarded-For`：代理后面所有请求都来自 `127.0.0.1`，按连接地址判会把本地访问也误杀。 > **职责边界**：身份认证不归这个插件，由前面的网关 / 反向代理负责。插件只做**同源校验**（Host 白名单 + `sec-fetch-site` + `Origin`）——那不是鉴权，是挡 CSRF：网关通常靠 cookie 认人，不拦同源的话，恶意网页可以借你的浏览器打 `/tieba/api/login/start`。 > > 相应地，部署时要保证 **DSH 的 webServer 只对网关可见**（绑 `127.0.0.1`，或防火墙只放网关的 IP）。否则绕过网关直接连端口，前面那层鉴权就白做了。 对外只交流 `application/json` 与 `image/png`（登录二维码），不提供文件下载或 HTML 通道；请求体上限 64KB。 > **cookie 是明文 JSON**（`~/.dsh-tieba/cookies.json`，`0600`），等价于你的贴吧登录态：别提交、别共享、别贴截图。 > > **别整份贴 `dsh --dump-config`**：它会把插件 config 原样展开，里面有 cookie 和本机路径。 ## 已知限制 - **只读**，没有发帖 / 回复 / 签到 / 关注 - 移动版单页上限 30 层，超过靠 `pn` 偏移翻页 - 登录态会过期（`BDUSS` 通常能撑几个月），失效时 `tieba_status` 明确报 `expired` - 「热门回复」区块未实现，目前用楼中楼代替 - 图片压缩依赖系统 `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe`：没装不会报错，只是跳过压缩 - 抓取受百度风控影响，请求间隔别调太小 ## 项目结构 ```text dsh-plugin-tieba/ ├── lib/ │ ├── index.js # 宿主半边：注册工具、挂 HTTP 路由 │ ├── client.js # 浏览器半边：手写的经典脚本，不是构建产物 │ ├── core.mjs # 内核：登录态、全量翻页、抽样、图片压缩 │ ├── browser.mjs # 定位磁盘上或系统的 chromium │ ├── server.mjs # 设置页用的 HTTP 接口 │ ├── config-store.mjs # 配置读写 │ └── paths.mjs # 运行期路径 ├── src/{cli,login}.mjs # 命令行与扫码登录 ├── locale/{en,zh}.json # 插件展示元信息 ├── scripts/check-browser.mjs └── cordis.patch.yml # bundle 层：插入 id: tieba 这一行 ``` ## 开发 改代码前先看 [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md)：那里有客户端产物的硬约束（必须是经典脚本，不能出现 `import`/`export`）、宿主侧不能静态 import `@deepseek-ai/*` 的原因、浏览器解析顺序、以及怎么验证改动。 一句话版本：`lib/client.js` 手写、保持 `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({id, factory})` 外壳；改完重启 DSH 才生效。 ## 彩蛋
真实使用现场（点开） > 截图里是贴吧用户的原始发言摘要，不代表本项目立场；昵称与帖子 id 都没有处理。

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# dsh-skill-evolve

A DeepSeek Harness plugin that notices when a session produced something worth remembering — a procedure that repeated, or a lesson a turn taught — asks the model whether it is worth writing down, checks that the model's evidence is real, and then ages the resulting skill out when it stops being useful.

It is not a memory system and not an autonomous self-improvement loop. It adds two things:

1. **An alarm clock** with two independent triggers: a repeated tool procedure, and a finished conversation turn. Both are rationed per session.
2. **A ledger** — verifies that a proposed skill's evidence actually appears in the transcript, and tracks whether the skill later helped or hurt.

Everything the model wants to save goes through a human unless `mode` is explicitly `auto`.

---

## Why it is built this way

Five findings from the research in `docs/` shaped every decision here. They are worth reading before changing the code.

**Do not run a second LLM to distil the conversation.** The model is already in the conversation holding the full context. A second pass pays for the whole transcript again to produce something worse. `@loserfox/distill` took that route and is broken on this host — it calls `ctx.subagents.start()`, which does not exist in DSH 0.2.1 (`SubagentRuntime` exposes `startActivation`). It fails silently in a `try/catch`, so it looks installed and does nothing.

**Prompt injection must be static.** The host re-assembles dynamic contexts every step, so any change to the injected text invalidates the prefix cache for the whole conversation. Hermes freezes its memory snapshot at session start for exactly this reason, and `hermes-agent-self-evolution` lists "no mid-conversation changes" as a hard guardrail. This plugin renders one hint string that stays byte-identical until a new procedure is worth mentioning, and renders `''` — fully absent, zero tokens — otherwise.

**Evidence gates beat prompt instructions.** `distill-kura` found that telling an agent "don't hallucinate" does not work; a deterministic check does. Every evidence quote submitted here is searched for character-for-character in the session transcript — but only in the lane its class claims, because a flat corpus lets the model quote itself and call it a tool result. Fabricated quotes are rejected and echoed back so the model can see what it invented.

**A skill that hurt should become a warning, not disappear.** `cass-memory` inverts repeatedly-harmful rules into `PITFALL:` anti-patterns: "Bad rules don't just get deleted — they become warnings." The same rule applies here at `invertAfterHarmful`.

**Zero uses is not proof of uselessness.** Hermes Curator's wording: "Zero uses is absence of evidence, not proof the skill is disposable." So nothing here deletes a skill. The worst outcome is `inverted`.

---

## What it does, concretely

### Two triggers, because they see different things

The plugin has two independent reasons to speak up, and they are complementary rather than alternative. This matters enough to state before the mechanics:

| Trigger | Sees | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| **Turn end** (`turn`) | Meaning: a correction the person made, a library pitfall, a dead end and the way through | Anything happening mid-turn |
| **Repetition** (`repeat`) | Structure: a multi-step procedure worth re-running | Everything semantic — it knows `read`,`grep`,`edit` repeated, not what was being fixed |

A repetition detector alone is blind to the most valuable thing a session produces, because "the pager API is zero-indexed" is not a tool sequence. A turn-end reflection alone never fires until a turn is over, so a long turn that repeats a procedure six times says nothing until it ends.

Qoder calls its version **Skill evolution suggestions** and this plugin's turn trigger is modelled on it: reflect when a task finishes, let the model decide whether anything generalises. That is affordable here for a specific reason — **the model is already in the conversation**. It is not a second pass over the transcript; it is one more instruction attached to a step the model was going to take anyway. The expensive shape — fork a subagent, replay the transcript, ask it to distil — is what `@loserfox/distill` did, and it is both costly and broken on this host.

Set `triggers: []` to disable both, `['turn']` or `['repeat']` to keep one.

### Detection

The detector sees **tool names only**, never arguments. A `read` of `a.txt` and a `read` of `b.txt` are the same step.

Four rules, each of which exists because the naive version misfired on a real transcript:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Non-overlapping occurrence counting | `a,b,c,a,b,c` is two procedures, not four overlapping windows |
| At least 3 distinct tool names | A real 487-call session spent its entire hint budget on `bash × 5 → todo_write`, which is "I ran commands and ticked a box" |
| No single tool filling half the window | Same habit, longer lens |
| The same habit is announced once | `read,edit,bash` and later `read,edit,bash,grep` are one workflow, not two |

Replaying a real 487-call coding session through the final rules publishes **0 hints** — correctly, because that session repeated habits rather than workflows. A synthetic session containing a genuine inspect→patch→verify loop publishes **1**.

### The hint

Rendered as one dynamic prompt context at order `121`, capped at `maxHintsPerSession` (default 4). It names the procedure, gives the occurrence count, and tells the model three things:

- call `skill_candidate_submit` with a **verbatim quote** as evidence, or ignore the message;
- **nothing will be written on your behalf** either way;
- **write down what failed**, not just the happy path.

That last line is the one that matters most. `self-learning-skills` puts it plainly: skipping a known dead end next session is often worth more than the win itself.

The hint is cleared the moment the model calls one of this plugin's own tools, so the next steps stop paying for text that has already been read.

Both triggers write into this one channel, so the prompt sees a single stable string rather than two competing ones. The turn reflection bypasses the procedure-dedup check (`distinct: true` in `hint.publish`): that check exists to stop one growing procedure being announced twice, and a reflection has no steps of its own to compare, so it would collide with the previous reflection on nothing but a placeholder marker. Its own throttle is the pacer's budget, which is the better fit.

When a reflection fires, the detector's findings ride along in the same message as supporting evidence — "you repeated these three steps" is a much stronger prompt next to "what did this turn teach you".

### The evidence gate

Four classes of evidence, each with different authority:

| Class | What it is | What it may support |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | Something the person said | "they decided / they asked for" |
| `tool` | Machine output | the only source for numbers |
| `action` | A tool that was invoked | "this was done" |
| `self` | The model's own narration | first-person judgement only, never a bare fact |

A submission survives only if at least one quote verifies **and** at least one `user` or `tool` quote survives. Self-narration alone is rejected with an explanation, because a skill is authoritative for future sessions.

Each class is checked against **its own lane** of the session, not against one concatenated blob:

| Lane | Built from |
|---|---|
| `user` | `user/message` authored by the human (`source.kind === "user"`) |
| `tool` | `tool/result` payloads — machine output |
| `action` | `tool/call` records: the name and the arguments the host dispatched |
| `self` | assistant prose only |

The revision that introduced lanes exists because a single corpus does not work. The model's reasoning, its tool calls and the machine's output all land in the same string, so it could quote itself and label the quote `tool` — a check that passes while proving nothing, which is the exact failure the gate is supposed to prevent.

Two details that look like nits and are not:

- **Tool arguments go in `action`, not `self`.** The text is a name and the arguments the host logged when it dispatched the call. That proves the call was made; it does not prove it succeeded, which is why `action` is not authoritative. Putting arguments in `self` instead would leave only tool names in `action` — `bash` is four characters, below the minimum quotable length, so the class would be unusable and the model would relabel the same fact as `tool`.
- **The model's `tool-call` block is not collected anywhere.** It is the model's *draft* of the call and exists whether or not dispatch ever happened. Admitting it would let a hallucinated call manufacture its own evidence.

Host-injected context (runtime reminders, skill catalogs, the system prompt) lands in a `system` lane that no evidence class may cite.

### Lifecycle

Four stages, driven by evidence rather than by a timer:

```
unverified --(promoteAfterUses loads)--> active
active     --(staleAfterDays without a load)--> stale
any        --(invertAfterHarmful harmful reports)--> inverted
```

**A load counts as a use.** When the model calls the host's `skill` tool with the name of a skill this plugin wrote, that is the one reliable signal that the skill was actually read — the catalog is served from memory, so nothing else fires. Each load increments `uses`, appends a `skill_used` line to the ledger, and refreshes `validated`. Counting is skipped for any name whose file does not exist or is not ours, so a model cannot inflate a counter by naming somebody else's skill.

Counting happens at dispatch rather than at result. Pairing a call with its result means holding a `callId → name` map and hoping the result always arrives; an interrupted call would silently drop a use, and an under-count is the failure that matters — it keeps a good skill `unverified` forever. The ownership check already rules out the common false load, so the residual error leans toward counting one that went on to fail.

This is *not* gated on `mode`. `mode` governs detection and creation; bookkeeping of skills that already exist is a separate question, and turning hints off does not mean the approved skills stopped being used.

`skill_feedback` remains the explicit signal — a person or the model saying "this helped" or "this hurt" — and it alone can raise `helpful` or `harmful`. Usage says a skill was *reached*; only feedback says it *worked*.

Counters live in two places on purpose: `registry.json` is the read path, and the skill file's frontmatter is the durable copy. If the registry is lost, the next load rebuilds the entry from the file — which is why every load rewrites the file rather than only rewriting it when the stage moves.

`inverted` is terminal until rewritten: the file gains a `PITFALL` section at the top and keeps the original procedure underneath, because a warning is only trustworthy if a reader can see what it warns about.

Confidence decays with a 90-day half-life, and one harmful report costs four helpful ones (`helpful - 4 × harmful`).

### Proposing a revision

A submission whose name matches a skill **this plugin** wrote is not a collision — it is a revision. The first version was written in a session that did not know what the current one knows; refusing the update is how a catalog ends up full of skills whose first draft is all anybody ever gets.

The revision records the base it was written against (a hash of the body, plus the lifecycle record). It is applied only if that base is still there, still owned, and still unchanged at approval time — so an edit made in between is noticed instead of silently reverted. Use counts and harmful counts survive the edit; resetting them would erase the evidence that says whether the skill is worth keeping at all.

A skill somebody else wrote is still a hard refusal.

### Candidates go stale

A queue entry is approvable only while the world it describes still exists. Four things can end that, checked every time the queue is read rather than on a timer:

| Reason | Triggered by |
|---|---|
| `expired` | older than `candidateTtlDays` |
| `source-missing` | the session it cites is gone |
| `name-taken` | a skill with that name appeared while it waited |
| `base-changed` | a revision whose target was edited or removed |

Stale entries are **reported, never deleted**: they hold the evidence and the body somebody already wrote. A stale candidate can be read with `--preview` and discarded with `--discard`, and resubmitting under the same name refreshes it.

### Approval is a handshake

`approvalMode: 'confirm'` (the default) splits approval in two:

1. `/skill-capture <name>` records the human's yes. Nothing is written.
2. The model writes the final body on its next step, via `skill_candidate_submit` with `final: true` — which gives it one more look at the current catalog before committing.

This is Qoder's behaviour and its wording: "task creation does not mean the Skill has already changed." The point is that a draft can age between being proposed and being approved, and the model is the only party who can notice.

`approvalMode: 'direct'` writes the queued body at once, which is what earlier versions of this plugin did. Both modes route through the same evidence gate: approval is permission to write *this draft*, not permission to write anything.

### The ownership fence

Every file this plugin writes carries `evolved-by: dsh-skill-evolve` in its frontmatter. A file without that marker is **never** modified — not by approval, not by inversion, not by feedback. Submission against an existing hand-written skill name is refused outright with an explanation.

### Storage

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Approved skills | `$DSH_HOME/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` |
| Pending candidates | `$DSH_HOME/plugin-data/skill-evolve/candidates.json` |
| Lifecycle registry | `$DSH_HOME/plugin-data/skill-evolve/registry.json` |
| Audit ledger (append-only JSONL) | `$DSH_HOME/plugin-data/skill-evolve/ledger.jsonl` |

Candidates live outside the skill root on purpose: an unapproved candidate must never be discoverable as a loadable skill.

---

## Install

From this directory:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile desktop add F:/dsh-plugin/dsh-skill-evolve
```

The package ships its own `cordis.patch.yml`, so the bundle registers itself. **Do not also insert it manually into the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`** — a duplicate loader entry id prevents the host from starting.

Then restart the host (a Host restart is enough) and confirm the plugin loaded:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile desktop list --depth=0
```

To disable it without uninstalling, set `disabled: true` on its entry in the profile patch:

```yaml
- id: skill-evolve
  disabled: true
```

### Configuration

All fields are optional. The defaults are deliberate: **propose, do not write.**

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `suggest` | `suggest` = hint only; `auto` = write on submit; `off` = detect and log, never hint |
| `triggers` | `['turn','repeat']` | Which triggers are active; `[]` disables both |
| `reflectionCadence` | `3` | Human turns before the first reflection; doubles after each one |
| `reflectionMinToolCalls` | `4` | Tool calls a turn needs before reflecting on it |
| `maxReflectionsPerSession` | `2` | Hard cap on turn-end reflections |
| `minRepeatCount` | `2` | Occurrences before a procedure is reported |
| `repeatWindowMax` | `6` | Widest window treated as one procedure |
| `minWindow` | `3` | Narrowest window considered |
| `maxHintsPerSession` | `4` | Hint budget per session |
| `skillRoot` | `""` | Override the skill directory; empty means `$DSH_HOME/skills` |
| `maxCandidates` | `50` | Queue cap before further submissions are refused |
| `candidateTtlDays` | `30` | Days a candidate stays approvable; older ones are reported stale, never deleted |
| `approvalMode` | `confirm` | `confirm` = approve, then the model writes the final body on its next step; `direct` = write at once |
| `verifyCandidateSource` | `true` | Refuse to approve a candidate whose source session no longer exists |
| `promoteAfterUses` | `3` | Helpful reports needed for `unverified` → `active` |
| `invertAfterHarmful` | `3` | Harmful reports needed to invert into a warning |
| `staleAfterDays` | `90` | Days without validation before `active` → `stale` |
| `hintRequired` | `false` | Make the hint a `required` context (survives suppression) |

`mode: auto` is the only setting that writes without a person seeing it first. It is not the default and should not become one.

### Reflection budget

A fixed cadence spends its whole budget early. Replaying the real 15-turn session documented below with `reflectionCadence: 3` and `maxReflectionsPerSession: 2` fired both checkpoints by turn 7, leaving the last eight turns uncovered. The cadence therefore **doubles after each reflection**, which puts the second checkpoint near the middle of a long session instead of right after the first:

```
reflection 1 → after 3 turns
reflection 2 → after 3 + 6 = 9 turns
reflection 3 → after 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 turns   (only reachable if the cap allows it)
```

That is rationing, not throttling. The cap is what ultimately bounds the noise; the backoff is what makes the cap land in useful places.

### What counts as a human turn

The host writes four different kinds of `user/message` into a session, and only one of them is a person:

| `source.kind` | What it is | Counts as a turn |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | A person typing | yes |
| `agent-instructions` | The `AGENTS.md` baseline | no |
| `runtime-context` | The per-step runtime snapshot | no |
| `user-approval` | A tool approval receipt | no |

All four were observed in a real session log. Counting the injected ones would make every step look like a new conversation and fire the checkpoint continuously.

---

## Use

The plugin adds three model-facing tools and four slash commands.

### Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `skill_candidate_submit` | Propose a skill. Validates name, description, body, and evidence; queues it (or writes it in `auto` mode). Set `final: true` to write the approved final version. |
| `skill_candidate_list` | Show what is waiting for approval, including entries that went stale. |
| `skill_feedback` | Record that a managed skill helped or hurt. Drives the lifecycle. |

### Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/skill-review` | List pending candidates with their verified evidence |
| `/skill-capture <name> [--preview\|--discard]` | Approve, preview, or drop a candidate |
| `/skill-feedback <name> <helpful\|harmful> [note]` | Record an outcome |
| `/skill-stats` | Show stage, confidence, and use counts for every managed skill |

A typical cycle:

```
(a long turn ends, third human turn of the session)
[skill-evolve] This turn is a checkpoint. Before you answer, decide whether it taught you
something a future session would need...

  1. Did the person correct me, or state a preference...
  2. Did I hit a dead end and find the way through?...
  3. Did I learn a fact about this project or library...

→ model calls skill_candidate_submit with two verbatim quotes

(next session, in the CLI)
/skill-review                    # candidate is waiting
/skill-capture scanned-pdf --preview
/skill-capture scanned-pdf       # approves it; the model writes the final body
                                 # on its next step, which lands
                                 # $DSH_HOME/skills/scanned-pdf/SKILL.md

(later, after using it three times)
/skill-feedback scanned-pdf helpful
/skill-stats                     # scanned-pdf is now active
```

The repetition trigger produces a differently shaped message when it fires first:

```
[skill-evolve] The tool sequence below repeated in this conversation...
  read → edit → bash
  2× · 6 tool calls
```

---

## Tests

```bash
node test/run.mjs          # every suite
node test/run.mjs signal   # one suite
```

335 assertions across nine suites. They are plain Node scripts with no test framework, so they also double as executable documentation.

| Suite | Covers |
|---|---|
| `signal.test.mjs` | The four detection rules, including the regressions that motivated each one |
| `evidence.test.mjs` | Verbatim matching, the four classes, fabrication rejection |
| `skillfile.test.mjs` | Frontmatter round-trip, ownership fence, malformed input |
| `lifecycle.test.mjs` | Promotion, inversion, staleness, confidence decay |
| `hint.test.mjs` | Sub-run dedupe, per-agent isolation, budget, rendering |
| `reflection.test.mjs` | Human-turn detection, cadence backoff, substance filter, budget, rendering |
| `candidates.test.mjs` | The four staleness rules and the queue annotation that keeps a recorded verdict meaningful |
| `index.test.mjs` | The whole plugin against a fake host: detect → hint → submit → queue → approve → promote → invert, plus both triggers together |
| `gaps.test.mjs` | The three later additions end to end: revisions, staleness in a real queue, and both approval modes |

### Replay against a real session

`test/replay.mjs` runs the detector over a decompressed `session.v4.jsonl.zstd`:

```bash
node test/replay.mjs /path/to/session_dump.jsonl
```

This is the check that matters most, because the synthetic tests cannot answer "does this fire on a real conversation or does it bury the model in noise". Run it before changing any detection threshold — the current values were chosen from its output, not from intuition.

To produce a dump from a real session log:

```js
// Multi-frame zstd: decompress frame by frame, not in one call.
const raw = fs.readFileSync(path)
const offsets = []
for (let i = 0; i + 4 <= raw.length; i++) {
  if (raw[i] === 0x28 && raw[i+1] === 0xb5 && raw[i+2] === 0x2f && raw[i+3] === 0xfd) offsets.push(i)
}
const text = offsets.map((start, k) =>
  zlib.zstdDecompressSync(raw.subarray(start, offsets[k+1] ?? raw.length)).toString('utf8')
).join('')
```

---

## What this plugin does not do

Each of these was considered and rejected, with the reason:

| Not done | Why |
|---|---|
| Run a second LLM to distil the session | Pays for the transcript twice to produce something worse; the inline model already has the context |
| Fork a subagent to re-read the conversation | Same cost, plus the fork does not share the parent's prompt cache |
| Write a skill without approval | The default is `suggest`; `auto` exists but is opt-in |
| Delete unused skills | Zero uses is absence of evidence, not proof of uselessness; worst case is `inverted` |
| Semantic (embedding) deduplication | Needs a vector store and a threshold nobody can tune; the catalog itself is the dedupe surface |
| Search external skill marketplaces | Out of scope — install `dsh-skill-hub` for that |
| Edit `AGENTS.md` | A different, more invasive surface; this plugin only writes SKILL.md files it owns |
| Session-scoped temporary skills | Not needed: writing to disk and letting the existing `dsh-skill-filesystem` provider discover it is simpler and survives restarts |
| Open a new conversation to confirm a skill | Qoder does this because a skill is authoritative. This plugin splits approval in two (approve, then write with the catalog in view) but keeps it inside the running conversation — a fresh context would cost a whole prompt cache for a step the model can take anyway |

---

## Honest limits

- **The core hypothesis is unproven.** The value depends on tasks recurring. If your work is genuinely one-off, this plugin will correctly stay silent and be worth nothing. That is the honest failure mode, and it is better than writing 50 useless skills.
- **Detection is structural, not semantic.** It knows `bash,read,edit` repeated; it does not know whether the repetition was a good idea. The model supplies that judgement, which is why the hint asks rather than writes. The turn-end trigger exists specifically to cover what structure cannot see, but it can only reflect on what the model notices — a session that learned something and failed to articulate it teaches nothing.
- **The reflection competes with the answer.** It fires at turn end, which is exactly when the model is about to reply. Four calls per session is the whole budget, and each one is a judgement call the model may get wrong in either direction: skipping a real lesson or writing a thin one.
- **Quality cannot be verified on a single machine.** `SkillClaw` needs multiple clients voting to eliminate self-assessment bias. A one-person installation can track whether a skill was used and whether it was reported harmful, but cannot independently confirm it works. Treat `active` as "reported used", not "proven correct".
- **Decay is time-based, not evidence-based.** 90 days is a guess borrowed from `cass-memory`. It will be wrong for some people in both directions.
- **A revision can overwrite a good edit.** It is refused when the base hash changed, which catches the common case. It does not catch a concurrent edit that lands between the check and the write — the window is milliseconds, but it exists.
- **Writes are serialised in one process, not across hosts.** The candidate queue, the registry and the ledger each take a lock, so two sessions in the same host cannot erase each other's work. Two DSH hosts sharing one `DSH_HOME` at the same time are not covered; the failure mode is a lost candidate (recoverable) rather than a corrupt skill (not recoverable).
- **A tool is not a result.** `action` evidence proves the call was dispatched, never that it worked. A skill citing only `action` quotes is not authoritative, and a submission built only from them is rejected.
- **Prompt cache cost is real but bounded.** Each hint is a single stable string, cleared as soon as it is acted on, and a session may see at most `maxReflectionsPerSession + maxHintsPerSession` of them. The costs that are *not* bounded: every hint invalidates the prefix cache once when it appears and once when it clears, and a hint that arrives while the model is mid-response is paid for by every remaining step until cleared.

---

## Background

The research that produced these decisions is in `docs/`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `01-调研报告.md` | Commercial IDEs, open-source frameworks, DSH-ecosystem plugins, an 11×8 capability matrix |
| `02-可行性分析.md` | Host capability verification, F1–F7 requirements, risks, effort estimate |
| `03-Hermes与开源生态补充.md` | Hermes in depth: `skill_manage`, Curator, frozen memory snapshots |
| `04-开源实现横向对比.md` | 14 open-source implementations, four architectural shapes, five mechanisms worth copying |
| `05-设计方案.md` | The design this code implements, including what was rejected and why |

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
Kivotos

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Every DeepSeek Harness you run, from any computer or your phone.

Kivotos is an open source plugin for DeepSeek Harness (dsh). Open any of your machines' dsh from any other, with its full UI: sessions, approvals, models, settings, files, and terminal. It adds a phone layout to dsh and comes with an Android app. - **All your machines:** Switch between them from the dsh sidebar. What you see is the remote dsh's own UI, so everything works. - **Two ways to connect:** Tailscale, or a relay server you run yourself. A machine can use both at once. - **Untrusted relay:** The relay only forwards end-to-end encrypted data. It cannot read it or join your network. - **Phone layout:** Drawer sidebar, composer at the bottom, safe areas, light and dark. - **Android app:** The full dsh UI, with notifications for approvals, questions, and finished tasks. - **Self-hosted:** No account, no telemetry, no push service. ## Getting Started ### Prerequisites - DeepSeek Harness `0.2.1-rc.2` - [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) signed in to the same account on every device, or your own relay server ### Plugin Install it on every machine. In dsh, open **Plugins → Install a third-party plugin** and enter `kivotos`. Or from the terminal: ```bash dsh plugin --profile web add kivotos ``` Restart dsh. Your other machines appear under **Machines** at the bottom of the sidebar. ### Phone Install the APK from the [releases page](https://github.com/Rinai-R/kivotos/releases). On the computer, open **Machines → Pair phone** and scan the code in the app. ### Relay Run the relay with Docker Compose on a server with a public address: ```bash curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Rinai-R/kivotos/main/packages/relay/docker-compose.yml docker compose up -d ``` On the first computer, open **Settings → Remote access → Own relay**, enter the relay's address, and create a network. Register it on the relay by running the command the page shows after `docker compose exec relay`. Other computers and phones join with the invite link or its QR code.
